17.0: But what have I done with my life? Mrs. Ramsay thought, as she took her seat at the head of the table and looked down at all the plates making white circles on it. “William, sit by me,” she said. Then, wearily: “Lily—over there.” Paul Rayley and Minta Doyle had that; she had only this—a table stretching on forever, plates, knives. Down at the far end sat her husband, slumped all in a heap, frowning. Frowning at what? She had no idea, and she didn’t care. She couldn’t understand how she had ever felt any emotion, any affection at all, for him. Serving out the soup, she felt she was past everything, through everything, out of everything. It was as though there were an eddy—there—and you could be in it or you could be out of it, and she was out. It’s all over, she thought, as they came in one by one—Charles Tansley (“Sit there, please,” she told him), Augustus Carmichael—and took their seats. And all the while she waited, passively, for someone to answer her, for something to happen. But this, she thought as she ladled the soup, is not a thing you say.
17.1: She lifted her eyebrows at the mismatch—that this was what she was thinking, and that this was what she was doing, ladling soup—and felt herself, more and more strongly, outside that eddy. Or it was as though a shadow had come down, and, with the color drained away, she was seeing things as they really were. The room (she glanced around it) was very shabby. Nowhere was there any beauty. She would not let herself look at Mr. Tansley. Nothing seemed to have blended. Each of them sat apart. And the entire effort of blending and flowing and creating was left to her. Once more she felt the sterility of men—not with any hostility, simply as a fact: if she didn’t do it, nobody would. So she gave herself the small shake you give a stopped watch, and the old familiar pulse started up again, as the watch starts ticking—one, two, three, one, two, three. And so on and so on, she repeated, listening to it, protecting and coaxing the still faint pulse the way you might shelter a feeble flame behind a newspaper. And so, she decided, bending silently toward William Bankes—poor man! no wife, no children, eating alone in his lodgings every night but this one—out of pity for him, now that life was strong enough to carry her again, she started up the whole business. She was like a sailor who, a little wearily, watches the wind fill his sail and hardly wants to set out again, and thinks that if the ship had gone down he would have spun round and round and come to rest on the sea floor.
17.2: “Did you find your letters? I told them to leave them in the hall for you,” she said to William Bankes.
17.3: Lily Briscoe watched her drift off into that strange no-man’s-land where no one can follow. Yet when people go there, it chills those watching so much that they always try, at least, to keep them in sight—the way you watch a ship fading until its sails have dropped below the horizon.
17.4: How old she looks, Lily thought, how worn out, and how distant. Then Mrs. Ramsay turned to William Bankes with a smile, and it was as though the ship had come about and the sun had caught its sails again. Lily, a little amused because she was relieved, wondered: Why does she feel sorry for him? For that was the impression she gave as she told him his letters were in the hall—Poor William Bankes, she seemed to be saying—as if her tiredness had come in part from pitying people, and pity had stirred up the life in her, her determination to live again. And that wasn’t true, Lily thought. It was one of her misjudgments, the kind that seemed instinctive and seemed to spring from some need of her own rather than anyone else’s. There’s nothing pitiable about him at all. He has his work, Lily told herself. And suddenly, as though she had stumbled on treasure, it came back to her that she had her work too. In a flash she saw her picture. Yes, she thought, I’ll move the tree more toward the middle; that way I’ll get rid of that awkward gap. That’s what I’ll do. That’s what has been bothering me. She picked up the salt shaker and set it down on a flower in the tablecloth’s pattern, as a reminder to move the tree.
17.5: “It’s odd that you hardly ever get anything worth having in the mail, and yet you always want your letters,” said Mr. Bankes.
17.6: What utter damned nonsense they talk, Charles Tansley thought, and set his spoon down exactly in the center of his plate, which he had scraped clean—as though, it struck Lily (he sat across from her, his back to the window, squarely in the middle of the view), he meant to make quite certain of his meals. Everything about him had that same thin rigidity, that same bare lack of grace. And yet the fact remained that it was nearly impossible to dislike anybody once you looked at them. She liked his eyes. They were blue, set deep, and frightening.
17.7: “Do you write a lot of letters, Mr. Tansley?” asked Mrs. Ramsay. She was sorry for him too, Lily supposed—that was true of Mrs. Ramsay: she always pitied men, as if something were missing in them, and never women, as if women had something. Mr. Tansley answered curtly that he wrote to his mother; beyond that, he doubted he wrote a single letter a month.
17.8: He had no intention of talking the kind of nonsense these people wanted from him. He wasn’t going to let these silly women patronize him. He had been up in his room reading, and now that he had come down it all struck him as silly, shallow, flimsy. What did they dress up for? He had come down in his everyday clothes; he had no evening clothes to put on. “You never get anything worth having in the mail”—that was just the kind of thing they always said. They got men to say things like that. Well, yes, it was more or less true, he thought. From one year’s end to the next they never got anything worth having. All they did was talk, talk, talk, eat, eat, eat. The women were to blame. With all their “charm,” all their silliness, women made civilization impossible.
17.9: “No trip to the Lighthouse tomorrow, Mrs. Ramsay,” he said, to assert himself. He liked her. He admired her. He still thought about the man in the drainpipe gazing up at her. But he felt he needed to assert himself.
17.10: In spite of his eyes—but then, look at his nose, look at his hands—he really was, Lily Briscoe thought, the most charmless human being she had ever come across. So why did she care what he said? Women can’t write, women can’t paint—what did it matter, coming from him? Obviously he didn’t believe it; for some reason it was useful to him, and that was why he said it. Then why did her whole being bend down, like wheat in the wind, and only lift itself back up out of that humiliation by a huge and rather painful effort? She had to make that effort again. There’s the sprig on the tablecloth. There’s my painting. I have to move the tree to the middle. That’s what matters—nothing else. Couldn’t she just keep a firm grip on that, she asked herself, and not lose her temper, not argue—and if she wanted a bit of revenge, get it by laughing at him?
17.11: “Oh, Mr. Tansley,” she said, “please take me to the Lighthouse with you. I’d love that so much.”
17.12: She was lying; he could tell. For some reason she was saying things she didn’t mean, just to annoy him. She was making fun of him. He had on his old flannel trousers—the only ones he had. He felt coarse and shut out and very lonely. He knew she was teasing him for some reason of her own. She had no wish to go to the Lighthouse with him. She despised him, and so did Prue Ramsay, and so did the whole lot of them. But no woman was going to make a fool of him. So he deliberately turned in his chair, stared out the window, and told her, abruptly and very rudely, that the sea would be too rough for her tomorrow. She’d be sick.
17.13: He was annoyed that she had made him talk like that, and with Mrs. Ramsay listening. If only he could be up in his room, alone, working, he thought—among his books. That was where he was comfortable. And he had never owed anyone a penny; since the age of fifteen he had never cost his father a penny; he had helped out at home from his savings; he was paying for his sister’s schooling. All the same, he wished he had known how to give Miss Briscoe a proper answer, and that it hadn’t come out so abruptly. “You’d be sick.” If only he could think of something to say to Mrs. Ramsay, something to show her he wasn’t just a dry prig—which was what they all took him for. He turned toward her. But she was talking to William Bankes about people he had never heard of.
17.14: “Yes, you can take it away,” she told the maid shortly, breaking off her conversation with Mr. Bankes. “It must be fifteen—no, twenty years since I last saw her,” she was saying, turning straight back to him, as if she couldn’t spare a moment from their talk, it absorbed her so. So he had actually had a letter from her this evening! Was Carrie still living at Marlow, and was everything just the same? Oh, she remembered it as clearly as yesterday—going out on the river, and being very cold. But when the Mannings made a plan, they stuck to it. She would never forget Herbert on the riverbank, killing a wasp with a teaspoon! And it was all still going on, Mrs. Ramsay thought dreamily, drifting like a ghost among the chairs and tables of that drawing room beside the Thames, where she had been so very, very cold twenty years before. Now she moved among them like a ghost, and it fascinated her—as though she had changed, but that particular day, grown very still and lovely now, had stayed right there all these years. Had Carrie written to him herself? she asked.
17.15: “Yes. She says they’re putting in a new billiard room,” he said. No! No! That couldn’t be! A billiard room! To her it seemed impossible.
17.16: Mr. Bankes couldn’t see what was so strange about it. They were quite well off these days. Should he send Carrie her love?
17.17: “Oh,” Mrs. Ramsay said, slightly startled. “No,” she added, thinking that she didn’t know this Carrie with her new billiard room. But how strange it was, she said again—which amused Mr. Bankes—that they should still be carrying on there. It was extraordinary to think that they had managed to keep on living all these years while she had thought of them barely once in all that time. And what a lot had happened in her own life over those same years. Then again, maybe Carrie Manning hadn’t thought about her either. It was a strange thought, and not a pleasant one.
17.18: “People soon drift apart,” said Mr. Bankes. Still, he felt a certain satisfaction at the thought that, after all, he knew both the Mannings and the Ramsays. He himself had not drifted apart, he thought, putting down his spoon and wiping his clean-shaven lips with scrupulous care. Though perhaps he was rather unusual that way, he thought; he never let himself fall into a rut. He had friends in every circle. … At this point Mrs. Ramsay had to stop and tell the maid something about keeping the food hot. That was why he liked to eat alone. All these interruptions irritated him. Well, William Bankes thought, keeping up a manner of perfect politeness and simply spreading the fingers of his left hand on the tablecloth—the way a mechanic, in a spare moment, inspects a tool that is beautifully polished and ready for use—these are the sacrifices your friends demand of you. She would have been hurt if he had said no. But for his part it wasn’t worth it. Looking at his hand, he thought that if he had been on his own, dinner would nearly be over by now and he would be free to work. Yes, he thought, it is a dreadful waste of time. Children were still trickling in. “I wish one of you would run up to Roger’s room,” Mrs. Ramsay was saying. How petty it all is, how dull, he thought, next to the other thing—work. Here he was drumming his fingers on the tablecloth when he could have been—and he took a swift bird’s-eye view of his work. What a waste of time it all was, really! And yet, he thought, she’s one of my oldest friends. I’m more or less devoted to her. Yet just now, at this moment, her presence meant nothing whatever to him. Her beauty meant nothing to him. Her sitting at the window with her little boy—nothing, nothing. All he wanted was to be alone and pick up that book. He felt uneasy; he felt like a traitor, sitting beside her and feeling nothing for her. The truth was, he didn’t enjoy family life. It was in a mood like this that you asked yourself, What are we living for? Why, you wondered, go to all this trouble to keep the human race going? Is it really so desirable? Are we an attractive species? Not especially, he thought, glancing at those rather scruffy boys. His favorite, Cam, must be in bed, he supposed. Silly questions, useless questions, questions you never asked when you had something to do. Is human life this? Is human life that? There was never time to think about it. Yet here he was asking himself exactly that kind of thing, because Mrs. Ramsay was busy giving the servants orders—and also because, when he saw how surprised Mrs. Ramsay was that Carrie Manning still existed, it had struck him that friendships, even the best ones, are fragile. People drift apart. Again he reproached himself. Here he sat next to Mrs. Ramsay, and he had nothing in the world to say to her.
17.19: “I’m so sorry,” Mrs. Ramsay said, finally turning to him. He felt stiff and barren, like a pair of boots that has been drenched and then dried out, so you can hardly squeeze your feet into them. But squeeze his feet in he must. He must force himself to talk. If he wasn’t very careful, she would see through this betrayal of his—see that he didn’t care two straws about her—and that would be anything but pleasant, he thought. So he inclined his head politely toward her.
17.20: “You must hate eating in this madhouse,” she said, slipping, as she always did when her mind was elsewhere, into her social manner. It is the same as when a meeting breaks into a clash of voices, and the chairman, to restore unity, proposes that everyone speak French. The French may be bad; it may lack the words for what the speaker actually thinks; all the same, speaking French imposes a certain order, a certain sameness. Mr. Bankes answered her in the same language—“No, not at all”—and Mr. Tansley, who knew nothing of that language, even in words of one syllable like these, immediately suspected it of being insincere. The Ramsays really did talk nonsense, he thought, and he seized on this new example gleefully, making a mental note that some day he would read aloud to a friend or two. There, among people who could speak their minds, he would give a sarcastic account of “staying with the Ramsays” and the nonsense they talked. Worth doing once, he would say, but never again. The women were so boring, he would say. Ramsay, of course, had done for himself by marrying a beautiful woman and having eight children. It would come out roughly like that. But right now, stuck in his chair with an empty seat next to him, none of it had come out at all. It was nothing but scraps and fragments. He felt terribly uncomfortable, physically uncomfortable, even. He wanted someone to give him a chance to make his mark. He wanted it so badly that he squirmed in his chair, looked at one person and then another, tried to cut into their talk, opened his mouth and closed it again. They were discussing the fishing industry. Why didn’t anybody ask what he thought? What did they know about the fishing industry?
17.21: Lily Briscoe knew all that. Sitting across from him, couldn’t she see it, as if in an X-ray, the ribs and thighbones of the young man’s craving to impress, lying dark inside the mist of his flesh—that thin mist convention had spread over his burning urge to break into the conversation? But why, she thought, narrowing her Chinese eyes and remembering how he sneered at women—“can’t paint, can’t write”—why should I make things easier for him?
17.22: There is a code of manners, she knew, and its seventh article (possibly) states that on occasions like this one it falls to the woman, whatever her own work may be, to come to the aid of the young man across from her, so that he can bring out and ease the thighbones and ribs of his vanity, his pressing need to assert himself. Just as it is their duty, she thought, with her old-maidish sense of fair play, to help us if, for instance, the Underground caught fire. In that case, she thought, I’d certainly expect Mr. Tansley to get me out. But what if, she wondered, neither of us did either? So she sat there, smiling.
17.23: “You aren’t thinking of going to the Lighthouse, are you, Lily?” Mrs. Ramsay said. “Remember poor Mr. Langley. He’d sailed around the world dozens of times, but he told me he’d never suffered anything like it until my husband took him out there. Mr. Tansley, are you a good sailor?”
17.24: Mr. Tansley lifted a hammer and swung it high overhead; but as it came down he saw that you cannot crush a butterfly with a tool like that, and all he said was that he had never been seasick in his life. Yet packed tight into that one sentence, like gunpowder, lay everything: that his grandfather had been a fisherman and his father a pharmacist; that he had worked his own way up, entirely; that he was proud of it; that he was Charles Tansley—which nobody here seemed to grasp, though one of these days every last one of them would know it. He scowled straight in front of him. He could almost feel sorry for these gentle, cultured people, who one of these days would be blown sky-high, like bales of wool and barrels of apples, by the gunpowder inside him.
17.25: “Will you take me, Mr. Tansley?” Lily said, quickly and kindly. Because of course, if Mrs. Ramsay told her—and in effect that is what she did—“My dear, I’m drowning in seas of fire. Unless you soothe the agony of this hour with some balm, and say something nice to that young man, life will run aground on the rocks—in fact I can hear the grinding and growling right now. My nerves are stretched tight as violin strings. One more touch and they’ll snap”—when Mrs. Ramsay said all that, as the look in her eyes did say it, then naturally, for the hundred and fiftieth time, Lily Briscoe had to abandon the experiment—what happens if you are not nice to that young man?—and be nice.
17.26: He read the shift in her mood correctly—she was friendly to him now—and, released from his egotism, he told her how as a baby he had been tossed out of a boat, and how his father used to hook him back out of the water with a boathook; that was how he learned to swim. One of his uncles, he said, kept the light on some rock or other off the coast of Scotland, and he had been out there with him during a storm. He said this loudly, into a pause. They had no choice but to listen when he announced that he had been in a lighthouse in a storm with his uncle. Ah, Lily Briscoe thought, as the talk took this hopeful turn and she sensed Mrs. Ramsay’s gratitude (Mrs. Ramsay was now free to talk a little herself)—ah, she thought, but what haven’t I paid to get this for you? She hadn’t been sincere.
17.27: She had played the usual trick: she had been nice. She would never know him, and he would never know her. All human relationships were like that, she thought, and the worst of all (if it weren’t for Mr. Bankes) were the ones between men and women. Those were bound to be deeply insincere. Then her glance fell on the salt shaker she had set there as a reminder, and she remembered that in the morning she was going to move the tree further toward the middle. The thought of painting tomorrow lifted her spirits so high that she burst out laughing at something Mr. Tansley said. Let him go on all night, if he enjoyed it.
17.28: “But how long do they keep men on a Lighthouse?” she asked. He told her; he was amazingly well informed. And because he was grateful, and he liked her, and he was starting to have a good time, Mrs. Ramsay thought that now she could slip back into that dreamland, that unreal but fascinating place—the Mannings’ drawing room at Marlow twenty years ago—where you moved about unhurried and untroubled, because there was no future to fret about. She knew what had become of them, and of herself. It was like rereading a good book, because she knew how that story ended—it had all happened twenty years ago—and life, which came spilling in cascades even off this dining table, heaven knows where to, was sealed up there, lying calm between its banks like a lake. He had said they’d built a billiard room—could it be true? Would William keep talking about the Mannings? She wanted him to. But no—for some reason the mood had left him. She tried, and he didn’t respond. She couldn’t make him. She felt let down.
17.29: “The children are a disgrace,” she said with a sigh. He remarked that punctuality was one of the minor virtues, one we only pick up later in life.
17.30: “If ever,” said Mrs. Ramsay, only to fill the silence, and thought what an old maid William was getting to be. Knowing he had been disloyal, knowing she wanted to talk about something more personal, and yet not in the mood for it at the moment, he felt the dreariness of life settle on him as he sat there, waiting. Maybe the others were saying something interesting? What were they talking about?
17.31: That it had been a bad fishing season, and the men were emigrating. They were discussing wages and unemployment. The young man was laying into the government. William Bankes, thinking how good it was to have something like this to grab hold of when your private life was disagreeable, heard him mention “one of the most scandalous acts of this present government.” Lily was listening, Mrs. Ramsay was listening; everyone was listening. But Lily, bored already, felt that something was lacking. Mr. Bankes felt that something was lacking. Drawing her shawl around her, Mrs. Ramsay felt that something was lacking. As they all leaned in to listen, every one of them was thinking, “Please God, don’t let the inside of my mind show.” For each of them thought, “The others feel all this. They’re furious and indignant at the government on the fishermen’s behalf. And I feel nothing whatsoever.” But then again, Mr. Bankes thought, looking at Mr. Tansley, perhaps this is the man. You were always waiting for the man; there was always the chance. At any moment the leader might come along—the man of genius, in politics or in anything else. He’ll most likely be extremely disagreeable to us old fogies, Mr. Bankes thought, trying hard to be tolerant. He could tell, from an odd physical sensation, as though the nerves along his spine were bristling, that he was jealous—partly on his own account, but more likely on account of his work, his point of view, his science. And so he wasn’t entirely open-minded or entirely fair. For Mr. Tansley seemed to be saying, You’ve wasted your lives. You’ve got it all wrong, every one of you. Poor old fogies, you’re hopelessly out of date. He did seem rather full of himself, this young man, and his manners were poor. But Mr. Bankes made himself notice that he had nerve, and talent, and a remarkable grasp of the facts. Very likely, Mr. Bankes thought, while Tansley laid into the government, there’s a good deal of truth in what he says.
17.32: “Tell me now …” he said. And so they argued about politics. Lily looked at the leaf on the tablecloth; Mrs. Ramsay left the argument wholly to the two men and wondered why the talk bored her so much, and she looked down the table at her husband and wished he would say something. Just one word, she told herself. If he said anything at all, it would change everything. He got to the heart of things. He cared about the fishermen and their pay. Thinking about them kept him awake at night. When he spoke, everything was different; you didn’t feel, then, please God don’t let them see how little I care—because you did care. Then she realized that she was waiting for him to speak because she admired him so much, and she felt as though someone had been praising her husband and their marriage to her face, and she glowed all over, never noticing that the praise had been her own. She looked at him, expecting to see all this in his face; surely he would be looking magnificent. … Not in the slightest! His face was screwed up; he was scowling and frowning and going red with rage. What on earth was the matter? she wondered. What could it possibly be? Only that poor old Augustus had asked for a second plate of soup—nothing more. It was unthinkable, it was loathsome (he signaled this to her across the table) that Augustus should be starting on his soup all over again. He hated people eating after he had finished. She watched his anger leap into his eyes, into his forehead, like a pack of hounds, and she knew that any moment something violent would burst out, and then—but thank goodness! she saw him take hold of himself and jam a brake on the wheel, and his whole body seemed to throw off sparks, but no words. He sat there scowling. He had said nothing, he wanted her to note. She should give him credit for that! But after all, why shouldn’t poor Augustus ask for more soup? All he had done was touch Ellen’s arm and say:
17.33: “Ellen, please, another plate of soup”—and at that Mr. Ramsay had scowled like that.
17.34: Well, why not? Mrs. Ramsay demanded. Surely they could let Augustus have soup if he wanted soup. He couldn’t stand people wallowing in their food, Mr. Ramsay frowned back. He couldn’t stand everything dragging on for hours this way. But he had kept himself under control, Mr. Ramsay wanted her to note, revolting as it was to watch. But why make it so obvious? Mrs. Ramsay demanded. (They were looking at each other down the length of the table, sending these questions and answers back and forth, each knowing precisely what the other felt.) Everyone could see it, Mrs. Ramsay thought. There was Rose, staring at her father; there was Roger, staring at his father; another second and they would both be doubled up with laughter, she knew—and so she said quickly (and it was high time):
17.35: “Light the candles,” and at once they sprang up and went fumbling at the sideboard.
17.36: Why could he never keep his feelings to himself? Mrs. Ramsay wondered—and had Augustus Carmichael noticed? Maybe he had, maybe he hadn’t. She couldn’t help respecting the calm way he sat there, drinking his soup. When he wanted soup, he asked for it. Laugh at him or be angry with him, he stayed exactly the same. He didn’t like her; she knew that; but that was partly the very reason she respected him. And watching him drink his soup, huge and calm in the dimming light, monumental, lost in thought, she wondered what he actually did feel at such times, and why he was always so contented and dignified. She thought, too, of how devoted he was to Andrew—how he would call him into his room and, in Andrew’s words, “show him things.” And then he would lie out on the lawn all day, presumably brooding over his poetry, until he put you in mind of a cat watching birds; and when he had found the word, he clapped his paws together, and her husband would say, “Poor old Augustus—he’s a true poet,” which from her husband was high praise.
17.37: Now eight candles stood in a row down the table. After their first dip the flames straightened, and they drew the whole long table into view, and in its center a yellow and purple dish of fruit. What had she done with it? Mrs. Ramsay wondered. For Rose’s arrangement—the grapes and pears, the horny shell lined with pink, the bananas—made her think of a trophy hauled up from the seabed, of a banquet of Neptune, of the cluster of grapes that hangs with its vine leaves over Bacchus’s shoulder (in some painting or other), among leopard skins and torches flaring and drooping, red and gold. … Lifted suddenly into the light like that, it seemed enormous and deep, like a world where you could pick up your walking stick and climb its hills, she thought, and walk down into its valleys. And to her delight (because for a moment it made them feel in tune) she saw that Augustus, too, was feasting his eyes on the same dish of fruit: diving in, snapping off a bloom here, a tassel there, and then, having feasted, going back to his hive. That was how he looked at things, not the way she did. But looking together brought them together.
17.38: Now all the candles were burning, and the candlelight drew the faces on either side of the table closer and gathered them, as the twilight had not, into a party sitting around a table. For now the night was shut out by panes of glass, and the glass, far from showing any true picture of the world outside, rippled it so oddly that in here, inside the room, there seemed to be order and solid ground, while out there was only a reflection in which things wavered and melted away, as if in water.
